title: equals/hashCode contract
concept: If you override equals(), you must also override hashCode().

steps.title: Person class definition
steps.explanation:
`Person` overrides `equals()` so two objects with the same `name` are treated as equal.
The problem is that `hashCode()` is not overridden together.

That breaks the **equals/hashCode contract**:
if two objects are equal, they must have the same hash code.

Because of this, hash-based collections like `HashSet`/`HashMap` can behave inconsistently and fail lookups in surprising ways.

steps.title: Create your first Person object
steps.explanation:
`p1` is the first person object named "Alice".

One key point: we did not implement `hashCode()` ourselves,
so Java assigns a default object-based number (for example, 123).

That means another object with the same name can still get a different number.
This is the starting point of the HashSet lookup issue.

steps.title: Create a second Person object
steps.explanation:
`p2` is a second person object, also named "Alice".

But `p2` is still a different object from `p1`,
so Java gives it a different default hash code (for example, 456).

Now we have two objects that look equal by value,
but may have different hash codes.
This mismatch is why HashSet behavior becomes confusing in the next steps.

steps.title: equals() comparison
steps.explanation:
When we call `p1.equals(p2)`, the result is `true`.
Both names are "Alice", so by our `equals()` rule they are equal.

So it looks fine so far.
But this is the trap: `HashSet` does not start with `equals()`.
It starts with `hashCode()` to choose a bucket first.

steps.title: Create HashSet
steps.explanation:
Think of `HashSet` as many small rooms (buckets).
When storing or searching, it first uses `hashCode()` to choose which room to check.

So `equals()` is a later step.
The first gate is always `hashCode()`.

steps.title: Add p1 to HashSet
steps.explanation:
When we run `set.add(p1)`, `HashSet` uses `p1`'s hash code (for example, 123)
to pick a bucket and stores `p1` there.

Right now, only bucket `hash(123)` contains `p1`.

steps.title: calls contains(p2) (search fails)
steps.explanation:
Now `set.contains(p2)` checks the bucket from `p2`'s hash code (for example, 456).

But `p1` was stored in bucket `hash(123)`.
So it is looking in a different room and returns `false`.

Key point:
Even if `equals()` says two objects are equal,
`HashSet` lookup can fail when their `hashCode()` values differ.
steps.keyInsight: hashCode different = different bucket = find failed

javaMemoryState.warning: equals() is true but contains() is false!

quiz.question: What is the equals/hashCode contract?
options: If equals() is true, hashCode() must also be the same.
If hashCode() is equal, equals() must also be true.
Both should always return the same value
You only need to override one of the two.
quiz.explanation: Remember: if equals() is equal, hashCode() must also be equal! (The station does not have to be established)

misconceptions.why:
Data structures such as HashMap and HashSet are first classified (old name) with `hashCode`, and then secondary confirmation (address number) is done with `equals`.
If the district name is different, you will never be able to find your home.

keyTakeaway: When overriding equals(), hashCode() is also required. Take advantage of the IDE’s auto-generation feature.
